title: Narasimha
hook: offered any wish at all, a boy says no thanks
tomorrow: one wish, then. and the boy spends it on someone else. who?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Narasimha came through the gaps in the king's boon: the doorway, the dusk, the lap. But after it was over, his anger didn't cool.

A genie, a wishing well, birthday candles: there are plenty of stories about getting a wish. Here's one where a boy turns it down. Narasimha is still raging in the hall, and in the Bhagavata, even the gods won't go near him. So Brahma sends the one person who isn't afraid: Prahlada. The boy walks up and bows, and the lion grows calm. Ask me for anything, he says. And Prahlada says: I'd rather not.
screen: `EVEN THE GODS WON'T GO NEAR.` → `THE BOY WALKS UP.` → `ASK FOR ANYTHING.` → `I'D RATHER NOT.`

segments.voice: Prahlada explains. Someone who serves in order to get rewards, he says, isn't a servant. He's a trader, doing business. So he asks for one thing only: that no wanting would rise in his heart at all. Here's that view at its strongest. Love that keeps a receipt isn't quite love. If you only call your grandmother when you need money, she can tell. Prahlada wants a relationship, not a transaction. Now the other view, and it comes from inside the tradition too. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names four kinds of people who turn to him: the one in trouble, the one who wants to understand, the one who wants something, and the wise. And he calls all four of them noble. Here's that view at its strongest. A prayer can start in a hard place: a hospital waiting room, a lost job, a test you might fail. The Gita doesn't send that person away for asking. The asking is how the door opens. So which is it? The tradition keeps both. Prahlada's no thanks is honored as the high road. Krishna's welcome keeps the road open for everyone still on the way. And Narasimha doesn't settle it either. He hears the boy out, and then he says: one wish, anyway.
screen: `SERVE FOR REWARDS: A TRADER.` · `LOVE WITHOUT A RECEIPT.` · `KRISHNA: ALL FOUR ARE NOBLE.` · `ASKING OPENS THE DOOR.` · then, large: `ONE WISH, ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: If you have paper, write two short lines, or just make them in your head. On the first, one thing you'd ask for today. On the second, one thing you love that you'd keep loving even if nothing came of it. Sit with both; the tradition keeps room for each.
Narasimha: the man-lion who, calm at last, offered a child anything, and heard him say he'd rather have nothing.
Keep this one: Narasimha, where one boy asked for nothing and Krishna still calls the askers noble. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Hindus pray for specific help, in hard times or before exams and journeys; others keep a practice that asks for nothing at all; some do both.

fork.setup: a friend only prays when things go wrong, and feels like a fake for it. which answer gives both views their due?
options: Krishna calls the one in trouble noble; Prahlada shows where asking can grow.
she's right to feel fake; Prahlada says asking turns prayer into trading.

fork.reveal: the Gita welcomes the one who turns to Krishna in trouble. Prahlada's no thanks is honored as the high road, not a door shut on the askers.

original.note: Sanskrit: noble, generous. Krishna's word in the Gita for all four kinds who turn to him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good devotee never asks God for anything.
what it means: Prahlada asks for nothing, and Krishna in the Gita calls the askers noble too; the tradition keeps both.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata 7.10 (the servant who wants rewards is a trader) beside Gita 7.16–18 (four kinds, all of them udara, noble).

chat.says: Nani says don't pray for my exam scores, it's 'bargaining'. dad says asking is fine. who's right?? 🙃
options: both have a case: Prahlada asked for nothing, and Krishna calls askers noble.
Nani's right. the old texts all say asking God for things is just trading.

chat.meaning: Prahlada's no thanks is the high road; in the Gita, Krishna still calls the one who asks noble. The tradition keeps both.

Prahlada.meaning: the boy who kept remembering Vishnu

Brahma.meaning: the creator god, who grants the king's boon

Bhagavad Gita.meaning: Krishna's teaching to Arjuna, inside the Mahabharata

Krishna.meaning: Vishnu's form who teaches in the Gita

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 7.9 (no one dares approach the raging Narasimha; Brahma sends Prahlada; the lion is calmed)
Bhagavata Purana 7.10.1–7 (the boon offered; one who serves for rewards is a trader, not a servant; Prahlada asks that no desire arise in his heart)
Bhagavad Gita 7.16–18 (four kinds turn to Krishna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of gain, the wise; all are noble)

notes: Debate shape: two views inside the tradition, each given its strongest case (Prahlada's desireless devotion, Bhagavata 7.10; Krishna's welcome to all four kinds, Gita 7.16–18). The lesson does not settle it.

Confirm Gita 7.16 (arta, jijnasu, artharthi, jnani) and 7.18 (udarah sarva evaite, all these are noble; the wise one is dear to Krishna as his own self, left out here). Confirm Bhagavata 7.10.4 (the trader image) and 7.10.7 (no desire in the heart). Paraphrased.
